articles.title: Oleksandr Usyk is considering a return to cruiserweight, casting Tyson Fury's hopes of a trilogy fight into doubt
articles.summary: Oleksandr Usyk is planning to return to boxing next year, but is considering moving back down to cruiserweight; Tyson Fury had been gunning for a trilogy fight with Usyk after his clash with Anthony Joshua; Usyk has been the undisputed champion at both heavyweight and cruiserweight before
articles.body:
The great Ukrainian, an Olympic gold medallist, has been an undisputed champion twice over at heavyweight and prior to that also at cruiserweight.

After beating Rico Verhoeven in their WBC title fight in Egypt earlier this year, Usyk, unbeaten as a professional, vacated the titles he held.

He is anticipating returning to boxing, but could do so back down at cruiserweight.

"Usyk has already cleaned out the heavyweight division. Now he is considering a return to cruiserweight, his natural weight class, to make history again," Serhii Lapin, CEO of Usyk's promotional company Ready To Fight, told Sky Sports .

"He loves challenges, and this could be the next one he'd like to take on."

The possibility of Usyk moving down in weight casts into doubt a third fight with Tyson Fury. Britain's Fury has boxed Usyk twice before. He lost both bouts but has publicly criticised the judge's decision in his second fight with Usyk and called for a third.

Fury wants to box Usyk after his December mega-fight with Anthony Joshua, but the Ukrainian might be considering facing new opponents now.

If he wants to go undisputed yet again at 200lbs, he would have to target imposing champion David Benavidez, who fights Michal Cieslak for the WBC, WBO and WBA cruiserweight belts on December 5.

articles.title: Volkanovski se sincera sobre lo que le queda en las MMA antes de retirarse
articles.standfirst: El campeón de peso pluma no tiene pensado realizar muchos más combates a sus 38 años, por lo que busca enfrentarse a grandes nombres y cobrar un buen cheque
articles.summary: El campeón de peso pluma no tiene pensado realizar muchos más combates a sus 38 años, por lo que busca enfrentarse a grandes nombres y cobrar un buen cheque
articles.body: Alexander Volkanovski es uno de los peleadores más grandes que han pasado por la UFC. El GOAT del peso pluma viene de agrandar aún más su legado el pasado UFC 333 tras finalizar a Movsar Evloev, y ha declarado que su intención es subir a peso ligero a por el doble cinturón dejando vacante su título en las 145 libras. El motivo es simple, ya que a sus 38 años sabe que le quedan pocas balas en la recámara y quiere aprovecharlas al máximo. Hay pocas cosas que le queden por cumplir a Volkanovski en su carrera, pero una de ellas es esa doble corona. En una entrevista con Ariel Helwani, el peleador australiano ha dejado claro que a día de hoy lo único que busca es un buen cheque ante un rival de renombre, puesto que quiere preservar su físico y retirarse antes de que el deporte le retire a él. "¿Por qué hago esto? Obviamente, por el sueldo. Nunca más recibiré un sueldo como este, pero quiero cuidar mi salud y estar ahí para mis hijos. Estoy satisfecho con lo que he hecho, tengo la suerte de ser un peleador que ya no necesita hacer esto. Me tomo cada combate tal y como viene", afirmó 'The Great'. En los últimos días ha propuesto varias opciones a la UFC. Una pelea de retiro ante Justin Gaethje por el cinturón de peso ligero, un combate ante Arman Tsarukyan por el título vacante de peso ligero en caso de que Gaethje se retire, e incluso una revancha ante Ilia Topuria. Volkanovski sabe que en peso pluma no hay nombres tan mediáticos, por lo que sus últimos combate quiere que sean en una categoría donde cobre más dinero al enfrentarse a un peleador de renombre. Además, la cabeza es algo muy importante para él, por lo que no quiere prolongar su carrera demasiado antes de recibir un K.O. que le produzca daños irreparables. "Las lesiones en el resto del cuerpo no me preocupan, pero en lo que respecta a la cabeza no quiero arriesgarme. Un golpe fuerte en el cerebro, una conmoción cerebral y se acabó. Así es como lo veo. Estoy sopesando todas esas opciones", finalizó.

articles.title: Canelo Alvarez vs. Christian Mbilli Judges' Scorecards, Punch Stats and Prize Money
articles.summary: Canelo Alvarez is once again world champion after a unanimous decision win over Christian Mbilli to win the WBC super middleweight title at Kingdom Arena in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.
articles.body:
Canelo Alvarez is once again world champion after a unanimous decision win over Christian Mbilli to win the WBC super middleweight title at Kingdom Arena in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

Canelo got off to a strong start in the opening round. He didn't indulge in an all-out fire fight, but he won the technical exchanges in the first. Mbilli also let his hands go and scored on a few punches himself. It didn't take long for Mbilli to settle in, though. He picked up the pace in the second round and showed he might be able to steal some rounds.

Mbilli did a good job of making the early rounds competitive. Canelo wasn't able to pull ahead early in the bout, but he appeared to turn the tide as the bout reached the middle rounds.

Canelo opened up his repertoire in the sixth round with some hard counters to both the body and the head.

Mbilli's pace was an issue for much of the night. His best bet was to swarm the challenger, but he allowed Alvarez to set the pace.

Some controversy came into play in Round 8. Alvarez was dipping his head, but it was Mbilli who had a point deducted by the referee for punching him behind the head.

It was a break that Canelo didn't really need. As the fight wore on, Alvarez's experience and technical advantages became clearer. He pulled away on the scorecards and didn't look back.

Mbilli turned in a disappointing performance, but it did appear that he might have suffered an arm injury.

Regardless, Canelo wasn't truly pushed in the fight and wound up adding another championship performance to his resume.

Saturday was the first time we had seen Canelo in the ring since his loss to Terence Crawford in September 2025. Crawford took the undisputed titles, but was stripped of one and dropped the rest upon his retirement.

That opened the door for Alvarez to once again claim a championship that has been familiar to him for much of his career.

It also begs the question of what's next for him. He's 36 years old with 69 professional fights under his belt. Retirement talk is bound to creep in after every fight he has over the next few years.

To hear him tell it, he's got a few more big appearances in him, though. He knows there aren't a ton of years left, but he's also comfortable with what he's accomplished in the sport.

"If it were up to me, it would never be enough. But I think four or five more fights would be enough. I've already done everything I needed to do in boxing. I've done more than I ever imagined I would," he told Brett Okamoto of ESPN.

Alvarez still clearly has the draw to generate plenty of money. He reportedly made $47 million off the fight while Mbilli was paid $9 million.

There are still some interesting fights out there for him. A rematch against Dmitry Bivol would be a massive attraction for the sport. Canelo came up short in his bid for the light heavyweight title in 2022, but Bivol still holds those titles with recent wins over Artur Beterbiev and Michael Eifert.

Either way fans, should enjoy Canelo's fights while they still can and he's fighting at a championship level.

articles.title: Canelo Alvarez returns to beat Christian Mbilli and reclaim WBC super-middleweight world championship in Riyadh
articles.summary: Canelo Alvarez outscores Christian Mbilli to win back WBC title in Riyadh; Jaime Munguia came close to disaster but retained the WBA super-middleweight title, beating Nikita Zon; Watch Chris Billam-Smith fight Cheavon Clarke on November 7 live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
The Mexican superstar won the title beating Mbilli by unanimous decision in Riyadh.

Canelo was returning to boxing a year after his stunning loss to Terence Crawford and went straight in with a strong, previously undefeated world champion.

Mbilli did press Alvarez in the first half of the fight. He threw in busy bursts and moved Canelo into the ropes.

But Canelo began to exert increasing control of the action from the sixth round onwards.

With brilliant skill he used a right uppercut to open a path for a hard right cross. He grew more comfortable on the ropes, working with counter-punches, and his vicious uppercut made Mbilli wary.

In the eighth round Canelo finished a four-punch combination with a right to the head. Mbilli drove forward and all of a sudden the referee took a point off the champion for hitting round the back of the head.

Mbilli urgently needed to shift momentum. Instead Canelo turned the screw. Alvarez came off the ropes to work from the centre of the ring, drilling Mbilli with his right hook.

In the final round Mbilli struck in a good shot but backed off. Canelo even waved him in again, but Mbilli wouldn't respond.

Canelo pressed forward, and Mbilli smacked him with a hard right. Canelo wanted to finish fighting and blasted home an excellent right.

He made sure of a unanimous decision, taking the win 115-112, 116-111 and 117-110 on the cards.

Alvarez is a vastly experienced veteran, who's won it all many times over in his 68-bout professional career. Yet he was delighted, almost relieved to be a world champion again.

"It's so difficult to explain. It's something unbelievable," Canelo said. "Now after 21 years as a professional, 16 years ago I won my first title, now I won the title again… I want to thank everybody back home.

"I knew he was a strong fighter. He didn't throw a lot of punches because it's difficult to throw punches with me... I did perfectly," he added.

"I'm going to keep learning, I'm going to keep working hard. I'm going to take a couple of weeks off and then come back."

Jaime Munguia had to weather an almighty scare to carve out a unanimous decision win over Nikita Zon and defend his WBA super-middleweight title.

Zon, genuinely an awkward southpaw, found a home for heavy backhand lefts in the opening rounds. He drove Munguia to the ropes and into corners.

He was on the verge of knocking out Munguia in the sixth round. He led with a long left uppercut, badly hurting the Mexican. Munguia retreated but Zon swarmed all over him. He hammered Munguia but the champion refused to fall.

When Zon tired, Munguia hit back and he took clear control in the late rounds to win 16-112 and 117-111 twice on the scorecards.

Towering featherweight Rafael Espinoza easily dismissed replacement opponent Ricardo Blandon to retain the WBO world title.

He banged a flush cross into the top of the Nicaraguan's head which opened up a nasty cut along Blandon's eyelid. The ringside doctor pulled him out in the third round immediately after inspecting it.

Watch Chris Billam-Smith fight Cheavon Clarke on the stacked Zuffa Boxing 12 card live on Sky Sports on November 7.

articles.title: UFC Vegas 123 live results, highlights, play-by-play
articles.summary: UFC Vegas 123 results, highlights, live discussion and instant play-by-play, reactions and analysis.
articles.body:
Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) is live TONIGHT (Sat., Oct. 31, 2026) with UFC Halloween (a.k.a. UFC Vegas 123 ) , streaming live online via Paramount+ . The event goes down inside the familiar META APEX in Las Vegas, Nevada. Our main event on this Halloween event is Renato Moicano vs. Tom Nolan ( see betting odds here ).

It feels a little odd to see a UFC fight night land on Halloween. It would be nice if UFC did something to dress up for the occasion, but knowing them it will probably be business as usual.

Renato Moicano vs. Tom Nolan draw the short straw of being unable to go trick or treating with their kids this night ( are you? ). They are meeting in the main event, despite Moicano saying he was desperate to escape the APEX.

UFC Halloween's co-main event is DC's boy Jacobe Smith taking on the veteran Randy Brown ( on super short notice ). Smith has decimated all who have stood in his way so far. If he runs through Brown, then he's a real player at 170 pounds .

Rounding out UFC Halloween's main card is Ode' Osbourne vs. Cody Durden , Yana Santos vs. Luana Santos and Jean-Paul Lebosnoyani vs. Farman Hasanov .

The "Prelims" are headlined by Francis Marshall vs. Dakota Hope . The biggest match-up on that portion of the card is Zachary Reese vs. Mickey Gall , with Gall looking to avoid his fifth straight loss. Former OKTAGON two-division champ Lucia Szabova also debuts at this event. She fights Tainara Lisboa .

The rest of undercard includes Rodrigo Sezinando vs. Theodor Berggren , Julian Erosa vs. Jeong Yeong Lee ( in a retirement fight for Juicy J ), Nick Klein vs. Joseph Kropschott and Talita Alencar vs. Piera Rodriguez .

We are back in the APEX tonight and that means a return to our usual broadcast times.

UFC Halloween "Prelims" will begin at 5 p.m. ET .

UFC Halloween main card is scheduled to start at 8 p.m. ET .

All of Halloween airs on Paramount+ , which you can stream here .

The live blog here starts rolling below at 5 p.m. ET . Come in and say hi!

170 lbs.: Jean-Paul Lebosnoyani vs. Farman Hasanov

145 lbs.: Francis Marshall vs. Dakota Hope

170 lbs.: Rodrigo Sezinando vs. Theodor Berggren

145 lbs.: Julian Erosa def. Jeong Yeong Lee via knockout (punches) — Round 1, 1:31

185 lbs.: Zachary Reese def. Mickey Gall via unanimous decision (29-27, 29-27, 29-27)

185 lbs.: Joseph Kropschot def. Nick Klein via submission (triangle armbar) — Round 2, 1:25

115 lbs.: Piera Rodriguez def. Talita Alencar via unanimous decision (30-27, 30-27, 30-27)

125 lbs.: Lucia Szabova def. Tainara Lisboa via TKO (punches) — Round 3, 3:20 — HIGHLIGHTS

145 lbs.: Julian Erosa vs. Jeong Yeong Lee: Lee touched Erosa's glove and immediately punched him — dirty? Kind of. Nevertheless, Erosa and Lee went to war for as long as the fight lasted, but it was Erosa who nuked Lee with a right hand and put him to sleep with ground-and-pound. Happy retirement, Julian Erosa!

Official decision: Erosa def. Lee via knockout (punches) Round 1, 1:31

185 lbs.: Zachary Reese vs. Mickey Gall : Reese spammed body kicks for most of the fight, with Mickey throwing overhands as Reese left his chin exposed. Reese did a point deduction in the first round for an eye poke. The two basically just traded for the entirety of the fight, with Reese getting the better of the striking. Pretty forgettable fight overall.

Official decision: Reese def. Gall via unanimous decision (29-27, 29-27, 29-27)

185 lbs.: Nick Klein vs. Joseph Kropschot : Klein was doing on the feet, but every time he took Kropschot down, he got reversed and put in awful positions — and that's what ultimately ended him when Kropschot reversed him, locked Klein into an inverted triangle, and tapped him with an armbar.

Official decision: Kropschot def. Klein via submission (triangle armbar) Round 2, 1:25

115 lbs.: Talita Alencar vs. Piera Rodriguez : Alencar had Rodriguez in trouble a few times with her elite grappling, but other than that, Alencar got clobbered on the feet by "La Fiera." Rodriguez is now riding a four-fight winning streak, while Alencar's three-fight winning streak is over.

Official decision: Rodriguez def. Alencar via unanimous decision (30-27, 30-27, 30-27)

125 lbs.: Lucia Szabova vs. Tainara Lisboa : Szabova was the biggest favorite on the card, and while at points she didn't look like it, she ended up overpowering and breaking Lisboa to stop her with heavy ground-and-pound. Szabova is a great addition to the Flyweight division and one to keep an eye on.

Official decision: Lucia Szabova def. Tainara Lisboa via TKO — Round 3, 3:20

articles.title: UFC Vegas 123 video: Julian Erosa retires after wild 91-second comeback knockout
articles.summary: Julian Erosa said goodbye to MMA with a "fairytale" comeback knockout win in his UFC Vegas 123 retirement bout.
articles.body:
Julian Erosa ended his MMA career on a spectacular high at UFC Fight Night 292 when he rallied to knock out JeongYeong Lee.

After Lee (11-4 MMA, 2-3 UFC) stormed out of the gate and cracked Erosa (31-13 MMA, 10-9 UFC) with a huge punch and nearly finished the job inside the first minute, the veteran survived and slowed down the action. He quickly got back in the firefight, but Erosa was on the one to seal the deal as he dropped his foe with a clean shot then put him out cold with ground shots at the 1:31 mark of Round 1 on Saturday at Meta APEX in Las Vegas.

Check out the replay of the amazing moment below (via X ):

Moments before the knockout, UFC Hall of Famer Daniel Cormier questioned Erosa's decision to stand and trade. He was quickly silenced by Erosa, though, and called it a "fairytale" moment after seeing Lee put out cold

The 37-year-old Erosa had three stints under the UFC banner. He said now was the time to lay down the gloves, though, as he shared his retirement interview alongside his wife and child.

"I feel so amazing," Erosa said in his post-fight interview with Cormier. "" knew this was going to be my last fight, so I wanted to go out with a bang. I want to do this tomorrow, but I had to make the decision that was going to be my last fight, win, lose or draw. And I'm happy with that."

articles.title: Mbilli vs Alvarez: Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez reclaims world title with vintage performance
articles.summary: Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez reclaims the WBC super-middleweight title with a vintage performance against Christian Mbilli in Riyadh.
articles.body:
Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez reclaimed the WBC super-middleweight title with a vintage performance against Christian Mbilli in Riyadh.

Just over one year since losing his belts to Terance Crawford, Mexican pound-for-pound great Alvarez returned to action with a confident victory by unanimous decision.

The 36-year-old, in his 69th professional fight, showed trademark slick defence and counter punching as he outclassed Mbilli to win 115–112, 116–111, 117–110 on the judges' scorecards.

It was the 64th victory of four-weight world champion Alvarez's illustrious career, while 31-year-old Mbilli suffered his first defeat in 31 bouts.

"It's so difficult to explain," said Alvarez.

"It's something unbelievable, this feeling. Like my first title. Thirty-one years as a professional. Sixteen years ago, I won my first title. Now, I won the title again. I'm so proud."

Doubts had been raised in recent weeks about whether the event could safely go ahead due to the growing conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi movement.

Just two days before the fight, Saudi Press Agency reported the Civil Defence had intercepted two ballistic missiles over Riyadh.

Earlier in October, a missile strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.

While other sporting events in Saudi Arabia - including The Six Kings Slam tennis exhibition, the final round of the 2026 World Rally Championship and the 2026 Urban Cycling World Championships - have been cancelled, the combat sports world has not followed suit.

Cameroon-born Mbilli, who trains in Canada, was making the first defence of his WBC title after being elevated to champion in January.

Alvarez, meanwhile, was competing for the first time without a world title to his name since 2015.

Pundits had questioned whether Alvarez's skills were declining following defeat by Crawford and over a year out of the ring, but his response was emphatic.

Mbilli pressured Alvarez in the early stages, peppering him against the ropes, with the Mexican looking to land big counters.

Alvarez responded by dismissively shaking his head to shrug off their impact, before goading Mbilli into attacking again.

Although Mbilli was throwing more punches, it was Alvarez who was landing the harder shots, with a couple of big right uppercuts finding the mark in round six.

The pattern continued in the next few rounds, with Alvarez countering the busy but largely ineffective Mbilli, before the defending champion was dealt a further blow by being docked a point for hits to the back of the head.

From there Alvarez cruised to the finish line with Mbilli continuing to push forward but posing little threat to the Mexican.

Alvarez's defence and timing of punches was too slick throughout, and although Mbilli landed a couple of stinging right hands in the closing stages, it was in vain.

Alvarez did not mention who he wants to fight next in his post-fight interview, but hinted at a quick return to training.

"I'm going to rest. I'm going to keep learning. I'm going to keep working hard," said Alvarez.

"And right now I'm going to be a couple of weeks off and then come back."

articles.title: 'Phenomenal:' Jake Paul, Terence Crawford and more react to Canelo Alvarez's vintage win over Christian Mbilli
articles.summary: Saul "Canelo" Alvarez turned back the clock Saturday night — and the boxing world took notice.
articles.body:
Saul "Canelo" Alvarez turned back the clock Saturday night, and the boxing world took notice.

The Mexican superstar returned from a 13-month layoff to defeat Christian Mbilli by unanimous decision and reclaim the WBC super middleweight championship in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Alvarez delivered a vintage performance, using his experience, aggression and precision punching to get the better of the previously unbeaten Mbilli.

The victory marked Alvarez's first fight since losing to Terence Crawford in September 2025 , a defeat that raised questions about how much the 36-year-old former two-time undisputed champion had left in the tank.

Those questions received a strong answer Saturday, as Alvarez earned his first victory in more than a year and improved his professional record to 64-3-2 (39 KOs).

Among those reacting to the result was Jake Paul, who praised Alvarez's performance while once again teasing a potential fight between the two.

"Out of the ring for 13 months but still the same old Canelo. Respect," Paul wrote on social media. "Did take a lot of punches though. We will dance my friend, we will dance."

Paul and Alvarez were previously linked to a potential blockbuster boxing match before Alvarez signed a lucrative deal with Turki Alalshikh's Riyadh Season in 2025.

Other observers were similarly impressed with the veteran's showing. One reaction, from former British boxer, promoter and analyst David Coldwell, summed up the fight accurately and succinctly in just three words: "Old manned him."

See how the rest of the boxing world reacted to "Canelo's" win below.

articles.title: Jake Paul, Terence Crawford React to Canelo Alvarez Winning Boxing Title vs. Christian Mbilli
articles.summary: Canelo Alvarez's unanimous decision win over Christian Mbilli to capture the WBC super middleweight title drew praise from around the boxing world on Saturday.
articles.body:
Canelo Alvarez's unanimous decision win over Christian Mbilli to capture the WBC super middleweight title drew praise from around the boxing world on Saturday.

Jake Paul and Terence Crawford both congratulated Canelo for the victory on social media.

The performance by Alvarez was particularly impressive considering his last fight was over a year ago, dropping the undisputed super middleweight title with a loss to Crawford in Sept. 2025.

Canelo then underwent elbow surgery before he was able to return, but the 36-year-old didn't show any signs of rust against Mbilli on Saturday.

"It's so difficult to explain," Alvarez said regarding his emotions after the fight, per ESPN's Brett Okamoto . "It's something unbelievable, this feeling. Like my first title. Thirty-one years as a professional. Sixteen years ago, I won my first title. Now, I won the title again. I'm so proud."

He improved to 64-3-2 with the victory, while Mbilli fell to 29-1-1.

articles.title: It takes a village: How Manisha Bhanwala rose from Siwaha's narrow lanes to top of the world
articles.summary: JIND: In India, villages make champions. Daughters of the soil, sons too, emerging from all corners, remote and close, carrying the dreams of a nation.
articles.body: JIND: In India, villages make champions. Daughters of the soil, sons too, emerging from all corners, remote and close, carrying the dreams of a nation. For Manisha Bhanwala, that journey began in Siwaha, a village in Haryana's Jind district, the narrow lanes of which now lead to the doorstep of a world champion. Late on Friday in Kazakhstan's Astana, Manisha became India's first-ever woman world champion in wrestling, that ancient Indian sport.Despite its proximity to the Capital, locating Siwaha - a modest village with around 4,500 registered voters - can prove a challenge. The routemap app, a global go-to, probably found its Everest in trying to locate it once the vehicle turned off the Jind-Panipat highway. A million reroutes later, once inside the village, there was no need for navigation. Ask anyone for the world champion's house, and enthusiastic children or youngsters on motorbikes happily escorted you to her doorstep. The modest two-storey house, tucked inside a narrow lane, has become a landmark.Outside, Manisha's maternal uncle Nanha sat on a tractor, tending to the family's cattle in between entertaining the frequent stream of visitors. After a quick request to secure the family dog, we were escorted inside to find Manisha's mother, Meena Devi, and uncle, wrestling coach Vinod Kumar, soaking in the moment on a charpai."It feels as though everything has suddenly changed. Before her world championship triumph, hardly anyone visited our home," Meena says simply, the pride quietly evident, "Now, relatives, friends and villagers from neighbouring areas keep coming to congratulate us. Journalists have been visiting. Our daughter has brought recognition to the family and the village. She has made the country proud."Amid all the noise, what awaits the world champion in her little corner at home?"Kadhi chaawal, her favourite, along with pointed-gourd curry and our special homemade chutney," Meena smiled. "There is one little secret, too. She loves sweetened tea, even though sugar is not ideal for athletes. I will make it for her. Home-cooked food is waiting."It takes a village, and a mother's sacrifices shaped that journey. Initially, Manisha's father, Suresh wanted her to lose weight through sport. Meena even learnt wrestling herself so she could accompany her daughter to the Nidani academy and help when sparring partners were unavailable.Nanha attended to the family's cattle as Vinod, uncle Chand Ram and cousins Jatin, Lakshya, Mohit, Priyanshu and Suryansh joined in. "Manisha was introduced to sport around 2008-09. Her late father Suresh initially enrolled her in kabaddi at the Nidani sports school near our village. She gradually developed an interest in wrestling after watching me coach," recalled Vinod."After her initial training, she moved to an academy in Samar Gopalpur village in Rohtak, run by the late coach Devilal. That was where her wrestling journey began taking shape."The mention of their father, Suresh, and the courtyard fell silent. Manisha was preparing for the 2022 Asian Championships when he passed away. She had promised him a medal. She returned with bronze.For the world championships, elder brother Rinku suggested she carry their father's photograph on her phone. Manisha wanted something more personal: a specially designed jersey featuring her father's photograph on the front and a family photograph on the back. "She wanted him with her," Meena said,.Now, as the family awaits Manisha's return, Rinku struggles to describe the transformation. "It feels as though our entire family has been reborn. People who rarely visited are coming to congratulate us. Her achievement has brought recognition to all of us," he said.It is the elder brother who has stood by her like a rock. Nobody perhaps understands the sacrifices behind Manisha's gold better than Rinku. "I accompanied her to Samar Gopalpur, where I continued playing kabaddi while she trained in wrestling. Since I had been involved in sport longer, she would discuss every little detail with me," he said.In 2017, Rinku suffered a ligament tear during a circle-kabaddi competition in Mandora village, Sonipat. Two or three surgeries followed, but his sporting career never recovered. "I had to give up kabaddi. But I made a promise to myself that whatever I could not achieve as an athlete, I would try to fulfil through Manisha. I wanted to see her become a world champion," he said.That year, Manisha joined the Sashastra Seema Bal under the sports quota and trained at Chhotu Ram Akhara in Rohtak under coach Mandeep. Eventually, she quit the job because it left insufficient time for training. A subsequent Haryana govt sports-quota appointment as a coach at the same akhara allowed her to pursue wrestling while guiding younger trainees. The pursuit came with the personal cost, that all athletes are familiar with. Today, it all seems to have borne fruit.Siwaha's narrow lanes may still confuse Google Maps. But one address needs no directions now: the home of a daughter who carried her father's promise, her brother's dreams and her village's pride all the way to the top of the world.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: UFC Vegas 123 results: Tom Nolan makes the most of controversial referee stand-up, knocks out Renato Moicano
articles.summary: After a referee restart got him out of trouble in Round 2, the 26-year-old Australian hurt Moicano with a knee and finished him with elbows in the third. It'...
articles.body:
It was UFC Fright Night for Tom Nolan, up until referee Dan Miragliotta decided to step in.

In Saturday night's UFC Vegas 123 main event, longtime UFC veteran and one-time lightweight title challenger Renato Moicano had the 26-year-old Australian in a bad position late in the second round, working with Nolan's back on the ground with a body triangle locked in. As the action slowed, Miragliotta decided to stand the fighters back up, which was essentially a "get out of jail free" card for Nolan, who took full advantage.

The 6-foot-3 Nolan landed a thunderous knee in the ensuing moments that hurt Moicano, nearly finishing him in the closing sequences of the round. It didn't take long into the third for "Big Train" to complete the job. After landing another knee, Nolan used vicious ground and pound, including massive elbows to Moicano's temple, to put the Brazilian away.

The end came at the 1:28 mark of the third round.

When asked if he was surprised that Miragliotta restarted them to standing in that second round, Nolan said he wasn't.

"Nah, I mean, you heard the crowd — they didn't love it," he said post-fight.

Then he saw a replay of his work on the big screen and was distracted by the knee that hurt Moicano.

"What a clean cross right, ohhhh," he said. "Bro, it's like we f***ing prepared for that. City Kickboxing, best gym in the world, let's go."

With the victory, Nolan (12-1) has now won six straight fights in the UFC's lightweight division, dating back to a mid-2024 stoppage of Victor Martinez. When asked what he thought of his performance, Nolan coughed up the game plan.

"We were confident the later it went, the more I'd be likely to finish him," he said. "That's why on the mat I didn't want to risk doing any stupid s*** and getting choked out. It might've been boring for you guys for like a couple of minutes, but I ended up knocking him out, so it ended up being f***ing sick."

When pressed if he'd like to call somebody out for his next fight, Nolan deferred.

"To be honest, not really," he said. "This was the guy I wanted to fight. I made a callout for the fight, and my job was to deliver tonight. This is my job right now, and I performed so, yeah — look, whatever the UFC wants to do with me next."

For Moicano (27-8-1), it's back to the drawing board after his impressive victory over Chris Duncan at the Meta Apex in April. The longtime veteran, who has two fights left on his contract, has now lost three of his last four in the UFC.

In the co-main event, Jacobe Smith showed why he believes he's the best pure wrestler in the UFC's welterweight division . Smith kept his perfect record intact by using timely takedowns, nearly nine minutes of Octagon control and strong ground-and-pound to out-point veteran Randy Brown on the scorecards.

The judges all saw it 30-27 in Smith's favor.

It's the first time the 30-year-old former collegiate All-American has gone the distance in a UFC fight, yet it was dominant from pillar to post. With the win his record improves to 14-0, while Brown, who has now lost four of his last five fights, drops to 20-9.

articles.title: Canelo vs. Mbilli winners and losers: Canelo Alvarez, Jaime Munguia salvage an event that had plenty of issues
articles.summary: Who won and lost in Riyadh on Saturday night?
articles.body:
The eyes of the boxing world were on Riyadh, Saudi Arabia on Saturday night, as Riyadh Season put on a puglistic showcase titled, "Mexico vs. the World."

On a night when Saul "Canelo" Alvarez became a three-time super middleweight champion , who were the overall winners and losers of the event?

Alvarez is a world champion again, regaining the WBC 168-pound title 13 months after losing it to Terence Crawford .

It was Christian Mbilli whom the Mexican great defeated Saturday night, winning via unanimous decision and giving us a glimpse into what Alvarez has left in the tank .

Was it vintage Alvarez? No. But after a slow start in which he seemed content sitting on the ropes, playing possum and tucking up to Mbilli's attacks, Alvarez began moving his feet, catching and countering, and punishing the Frenchman's advances with sharp riposte and some clubbing, signature left hooks.

The control came in the second half of the fight. Alvarez — like he has done to a litany of fighters — decided Mbilli couldn't hurt him and, importantly, couldn't beat him to the punch in the important exchanges. In the championship rounds, Alvarez was even able to turn the tables and become the front-foot fighter.

Is Mbilli a bona fide world-class super middleweight? Probably not, but Alvarez can only beat who is put in front of him. And looking at the current crop of super middleweight contenders, there are plenty more names — and paychecks — for the Mexican to work through on what could turn into a pre-retirement tour.

What's next for Alvarez? Well you'll have to ask Turki Alalshikh. "Canelo" still has a fight left on his contract with Saudi Arabia, so you'd imagine boxing's most influential matchmaker will want something significant and head-turning for his prized asset.

Will he find that scanning down the list of current super middleweight contenders? The WBC's interim champion is Lester Martinez. The other champions are Osleys Iglesias and Jaime Munguia, whom Alvarez already defeated. So perhaps not.

Knowing some of the curveballs that Alalshikh has thrown our way over the last couple of years, it would be a shock if he was eyeing up an all-Mexican affair between Alvarez and David Benavidez — a fight that has been on a long-running collision course, made harder in recent years by Benavidez's recent jumps in weight.

But if Alvarez can't get the dance partners, expect him to start targeting some of the arenas left on his boxing bucket list — namely, Mexico City's historic Estadio Azteca .

Munguia is fun, isn't he? They say that skills pay the bills, but entertainment sells tickets.

Munguia clung to this WBA super middleweight title, surviving scare after scare against the unheralded Nikita Zon , narrowly avoiding a huge upset after repeatedly getting hurt.

And did we witness a 2026 Round of the Year contender in Round 6 as both men traded near fight-ending blows after their own barrages of sustained attacks?

It's perhaps a damning indictment of the 168-pound landscape that Munguia finds himself sitting near the top of it. There are glaring holes in his game, but few can question his willingness to have a go. He is as game as they come and, with the title still draped over his shoulder, should make for some interesting defenses.

Bektemir Melikuziev is likely next in line. But after Saturday night, Munguia hardly looks like an immovable obstacle. There will be plenty of contenders watching the tape and fancying their chances.

But a win is a win, and Munguia wakes up on Sunday morning with a sore head as a world champion — and with a queue forming at his door.

It's sort of an unwritten rule in boxing: When you're handed a late-replacement opponent, you have to get the fighter out of there.

That's exactly what Rafael Espinoza did to Carlos Blandon in the fifth defense of his WBO featherweight crown , stopping the challenger in three rounds after the ringside doctor advised the referee to stop the fight following a cut to Blandon's left eye.

It was a sharp, well-timed right hand that did the damage to the scarred eye socket of Blandon, giving Espinoza his 29th career win alongside his 24th stoppage to stay unbeaten.

In truth, it won't be a fight that will live long in the memory. Espinoza will have been a featherweight world champion for three years once we hit December and bigger fights and harder tests are now well overdue.

The all-singing, all-dancing Espinoza said post-fight that he wants unification fights at 126 pounds, and he also wants to fight Naoya Inoue in Japan — but he didn't exactly shout it to the hilltops.

He spent more time signing to the crowd than he did giving any further details of how his 2027 might play out. And who could blame him when you have a voice like that?

Team Mexico got off to a pretty slow start on the night, rubber-stamped by the big upset of the evening as David Picasso lost via split decision to Carl Jammes Martin.

And you'd have to have a heart of stone to deny the dancing of "Wonder Boy" as he grabbed the WBC Silver featherweight title from Picasso despite suffering a knockdown in Round 7.

It was a nip-and-tuck affair across a very competitive 10 rounds. It could have gone either way on the scorecards, but Martin got the nod and extended his unbeaten professional record to 29-0 (21 KOs).

Martin has spent a majority of his career fighting in his native Philippines, but now with a recognized name on his record, he will attract a lot more attention in the 126-pound division.

I'm reluctant to lay into Mbilli too much.

DAZN's commentary team was very critical of the Frenchman's unwillingness to engage with Alvarez down the stretch, gift-wrapping his WBC world title to the man who has owned it twice before.

But it's a tale as old as time. It's easy to sit there and tell a fighter to just go for broke — but if you can't find the openings to land these bombs, then you're going to get found out with counters quickly.

"He didn't throw a lot of punches, because it's hard to throw punches with me," Alvarez said post-fight in the ring, stressing that point.

Fellow super middleweight Gabriel Rosado posted on X : "You can obviously see there's a tear on Mbilli [sic] left bicep," and perhaps some excuses will come out in the days that follow. But when Alvarez is on, you have to be pretty close to perfect to beat him.

Mbilli is only 31 years old and will rebound from this. It's the first loss of his career and he had enough moments in Saturday's fight to bolster his career-highlights package.

It's Riyadh Season, baby — and for boxing, it's a case of everybody acting like nothing is happening and nothing is wrong . It's that meme of the dog sitting having a cup of coffee while his house burns in the background.

That shouldn't be a surprise. Boxing is, after all, the black sheep of sport and often finds itself veering into its own lane, unbothered by the pile-up it leaves behind.

We knew the story heading into this weekend's card: The Iran-backed Houthi rebels of Yemen are at war with a Saudi-led coalition, and Riyadh — more specifically King Khalid International Airport — was turned into a battleground across October.

But despite the cancellation or postponement of other sporting events due to take place in Riyadh, "Mexico vs. the World" went ahead.

Alalshikh, the head honcho of Riyadh Season, was disturbingly silent.

That silence is the most telling part of all. There was very little in the way of public reassurance and little explanation of why this particular event is proceeding while others have been pulled from the calendar. Instead, the boxing machine kept rolling, seemingly determined to punch through the noise outside the ring.

And that is where the sport's peculiar relationship with Saudi Arabia becomes difficult to ignore. Boxing has spent the past few years following the money to Riyadh, happily accepting the enormous purses, grandiose production and promise of fights that once seemed impossible to make.

But when the conversation shifts from spectacle to security, the answers become harder to find.

The audience looked patchy and uninterested in Riyadh. This event alienated thousands of fans that could — and should have — witnessed an Alvarez fight live. That's if sense prevailed and Saturday's event was relocated west to the United States or perhaps Mexico.

Let's get it straight: "Bek the Bully" got screwed in October.

The dangerous Uzbek, now 30 years old, should have been fighting Jaime Munguia on this card for Munguia's WBA crown at 168 pounds, but instead Melikuziev got ignored by the champion and the sanctioning body.

Munguia was ordered to face No. 1 contender Melikuziev next, with the WBA giving both camps until Oct. 21 to reach an agreement — but the champion and his team refused, opting to invite Zon to Riyadh instead to challenge for the title.

The WBA claimed to have not approved the fight and promised to "review the situation," but in typical sanctioning body style, it stayed quiet afterward, leaving it until fight week for the chips to fall.

According to Mike Coppinger on the DAZN broadcast, Melikuziev's team accepted a step-aside deal late this week, on the condition that Melikuziev faces Munguia within the next 90 days. The agreement also includes a 60-40 purse split in favor of the champion.

After weeks of administrative limbo, it seems we've found a resolution. But would anyone really be surprised if this fight fell through again?

And considering Munguia's shortcomings against Zon on the night, Melikuziev will be going to bed tonight convinced he would have finished the job that the Russian was able to start.

After Espinoza stopped Blandon, we headed back into the DAZN studios to find Chris Mannix describing the stoppage as "extremely premature."

Now, I am no doctor. And I'm pretty sure Chris Mannix isn't a doctor, either.

But I do know who is a doctor. And that's Neil Scott, the chief medical officer of the British Boxing Board of Control from 2017 up until June of this year. Scott is still on the British Boxing Board of Control medical panel and independently contracted by the sport's leading promoters.

"I wonder what the doctor was looking at," Mannix continued. "How much experience does that doctor have in professional boxing? Because that is not the kind of cut that is deep enough to stop any fight, let alone a championship fight."

Scott's judgment should be trusted by fighters who put their lives on the line.

I get it: Mannix is paid to give his opinion. But Scott is paid to look after the health and safety of boxers — and I know which I deem more important.

Say what you want about Zuffa Boxing and Dana White — and believe me, I have — but there were moments Saturday when you couldn't help wishing their production team had been handed the keys.

White has made no secret of his desire to bring some UFC-style urgency to boxing broadcasts. That means cutting out the seemingly endless gaps between fights, ditching the unnecessary filler and, above all, keeping the action moving.

After watching fewer than five rounds of boxing across two-and-a-half hours of the broadcast before Munguia vs. Zon, you can understand the appeal.

To be fair, Kate Scott, Malik Scott and Mannix deserve some credit for keeping the conversation ticking over during the lengthy wait. They had an arena full of super middleweights to call upon for interviews, at least, as everyone patiently waited for — and I quote — "Turki Alalshikh to take his seat."

A novel reason to keep a boxing audience waiting, if nothing else.

France's Christian Mbilli (L) will not look back fondly on his performance against Alvarez. (FAYEZ NURELDINE via Getty Images)
Turki Alalashikh celebrates with Saúl "Canelo" Álvarez. (Mark Robinson via Getty Images)

articles.title: Nolan noquea a Moicano y confirma el cambio generacional en el peso ligero de la UFC
articles.standfirst: El peleador australiano sobrevivió a las habilidades en jiu-jitsu del brasileño para finalizarlo en una cartelera llena de grandes momentos
articles.summary: El peleador australiano sobrevivió a las habilidades en jiu-jitsu del brasileño para finalizarlo en una cartelera llena de grandes momentos
articles.body: Esta pasada madrugada la UFC ha vuelto al APEX de Las Vegas con una cartelera para paladares intrépidos, donde la guinda del pastel la ha puesto Tom Nolan (12-1) al noquear a Renato Moicano (21-8-1) en el tercer asalto para dar un golpe sobre la mesa en el pelo ligero y confirmar un cambio generacional en la categoría. Nolan se estrenó en el top 15 tras superar a Fares Ziam en su última pelea, pero en esta ocasión tenía en frente la primera prueba de fuego de su carrera. De hecho, Tom reconoció antes del duelo que era admirador de Moicano, aunque el brasileño no quiso entrar en su juego de halagos e hizo gala de su famosa personalidad afirmando que él solo quiere dinero. Renato no venía a hacer amigos, y lo demostró en los dos primeros asaltos dominando en el suelo a Nolan y tomando su espalda. Sin embargo, el árbitro decidió levantar a ambos peleadores incomprensiblemente en una de esas ocasiones en las que el brasileño estaba en la espalda del australiano, lo que fue el principio del fin. Tom dañó a Moicano con una rodilla, y en el tercer asalto le finalizó con otro aluvión de golpes y ground and pound que le asegurar enfrentarse a un top 10 en su siguiente aparición. Otro de los principales protagonistas fue Jacobe Smith (14-0) en el evento co estelar, ya que dominó a Randy Brown (20-9) haciendo gala de sus habilidades en el grappling para superar con nota su primer gran reto en la división de peso wélter. Todo gran peleador debe pasar por el jamaciano en esta división, y el estadounidense le dio un correctivo a pesar de ver frenada su racha de finalizaciones en la compañía -cuatro consecutivas-. En el resto de la cartelera estelar hay que destacar la victoria de Luana Santos (12-2) ante Yana Santos (17-9, 1NC) que le deja a las puertas de una oportunidad titular en peso gallo femenino, el triunfo de todo un veterano como Cody Durden (19-11-1) ante Ode' Osbourne (13-10, 2 NC) por decisión unánime, o la actuación de Jean-Paul Lebosloyani (12-2) ante Farman Hasanov (5-1) que obligó al árbitro a parar la pelea por un aparatoso corte en el párpado del azerbayano. En las preliminares, Rodrigo Sezinando (10-2) también obligó al médico a parar su combate ante Theodor Berggren (8-5) por otro preocupante corte, mientras que Julian Erosa (32-14) se retiró de las MMA por todo lo alto con un K.O. ante JeonYeong Lee (11-4) en el primer asalto después de estar prácticamente finalizado. Además, Joe Kropschot (10-3) debutó a lo grande en la UFC con una sumisión a Nick Klein (6-4) después de ganarse su contrato en las Dana White's contender Series hace unas semanas, mientras que Lucia Szabova (13-0) también completó con éxito su primera pelea en la compañía y mantuvo su invicto tras finalizar a Tainara Lisboa (7-5) en el tercer round. Rodrigo Sezinando derrotó a Theodor Berggren por nocaut técnico (detención médica, corte) – Asalto 2, 5:00 Julian Erosa venció a JeongYeong Lee por nocaut (golpes) – Asalto 1, 1:31 Zach Reese venció a Mickey Gall por decisión unánime (29-27, 29-27, 29-27) Joe Kropschot venció a Nick Klein por sumisión (barra de brazo) – Asalto 2, 1:25 Piera Rodríguez derrotó a Talita Alencar vía decisión unánime (30-27, 30-27, 30-27) Lucía Szabova derrotó a Tainara Lisboa por nocaut técnico (golpes) – Ronda 3, 3:20
